predictions.explanation:
As of November 30, 2025, it is too early to judge a prediction whose explicit horizon is **5–10 years after May 2023** (i.e., roughly 2028–2033). We are only about 2.5 years into that window, so the core claim about what will or will not be possible for regulators by that time cannot yet be tested.

What we can say so far:

- **On-device / edge models are clearly advancing, but not dominant for frontier capabilities.** Apple’s “Apple Intelligence” strategy uses a relatively small ~3B-parameter model on-device plus larger models in a privacy-preserving cloud, illustrating a hybrid approach rather than a full shift of powerful models entirely to the edge.
  Apple emphasizes that many features run on-device, but more complex tasks are still offloaded to server-side models via Private Cloud Compute. ([apple.com](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2024/06/introducing-apple-intelligence-for-iphone-ipad-and-mac/?utm_source=openai))

- **Regulatory systems are still in the process of being built, not demonstrably obsolete yet.** The EU AI Act, approved in 2024 and entering phased effect starting August 2025, creates obligations specifically for general‑purpose / foundation models (called GPAI models), focusing on transparency, safety, and risk controls rather than trying to track every individual device instance. ([ibanet.org](https://www.ibanet.org/the-regulation-of-foundation-models-in-the-eu-ai-act?utm_source=openai))  Enforcement and guidance are still being rolled out and even debated (e.g., calls to delay enforcement and soften rules), but there is not yet clear evidence that regulators *in principle* cannot monitor major model families or providers. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/media-telecom/will-eu-delay-enforcing-its-ai-act-2025-07-03/?utm_source=openai))

- **The prediction’s key test (“it will be effectively impossible for regulators to comprehensively track, audit, and approve which models are being run on which machines”) is inherently about the *end state* of a technological and regulatory race.** Current trends (rapid open-source proliferation and stronger on-device hardware, alongside regulatory experimentation) could plausibly support Friedberg’s concern, but by 2025 we do not yet have decisive evidence either way.

Because the specified 2028–2033 timeframe has not arrived and present evidence does not conclusively show that comprehensive regulatory oversight over models-on-edge is either definitively possible or definitively impossible, the prediction’s truth value cannot yet be determined.

predictions.explanation:
Evidence suggests that Jason’s *directional* prediction—that the official mobile app would drive about an order‑of‑magnitude jump in both users and usage—has essentially come true, even if the user count has not landed exactly at 10×.

**Baseline (pre‑app):**
- By January 2023, before any official mobile app, ChatGPT had already surpassed **100 million monthly active users**, widely reported as the fastest growth for a consumer app at the time. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ChatGPT?utm_source=openai))
- Web traffic was about **616 million visits in January 2023** and climbed to around **1.8 billion monthly visits by April–May 2023**, just before and around the iOS app launch. ([nerdynav.com](https://nerdynav.com/chatgpt.statistics/?utm_source=openai))

**Post‑app user growth:**
- OpenAI CEO Sam Altman announced **100 million weekly active users** in November 2023. ([techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2023/11/06/Openais-Chatgpt-Now-Has-100-Million-Weekly-Active-Users/?utm_source=openai))
- Weekly active users then grew to **300 million by December 2024** and **400 million by February 2025**. ([theverge.com](https://www.theverge.com/2024/12/4/24313097/chatgpt-300-million-weekly-users?utm_source=openai))
- By DevDay 2025, Altman reported **around 800 million weekly active users**, with Business Insider and other outlets repeating that figure. ([businessinsider.com](https://www.businessinsider.com/chatgpt-users-openai-sam-altman-devday-llm-artificial-intelligence-2025-10?utm_source=openai))  Relative to the ~100M active‑user baseline in early 2023, that’s roughly a **7–8×** increase in recurring users.

**Post‑app usage (volume) growth:**
- Within a week of its late‑2022 launch, ChatGPT was handling on the order of **10 million queries per day**. ([digitalinformationworld.com](https://www.digitalinformationworld.com/2025/05/chatgpt-stats-in-numbers-growth-usage-and-global-impact.html?utm_source=openai))
- By December 2024, OpenAI said ChatGPT was already processing **over 1 billion messages per day**, a ≥100× jump versus those early levels. ([theverge.com](https://www.theverge.com/2024/12/4/24313097/chatgpt-300-million-weekly-users?utm_source=openai))
- In **July 2025**, OpenAI disclosed that ChatGPT now handles about **2.5 billion prompts every day**, a 150% increase over late‑2024 usage. ([timesofindia.indiatimes.com](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/technology/tech-news/chatgpt-now-handles-2-5-billion-user-prompts-daily-confirms-company/articleshow/122836218.cms?utm_source=openai))  That is clearly **well over a 10× increase** in usage volume compared with the pre‑app era.

**Role of the mobile app:**
- The official iOS app launched in the US on **May 18, 2023**, and expanded to **dozens of countries and then 152+ countries** by early June; Android followed in August 2023. ([iqiglobal.com](https://iqiglobal.com/blog/chatgpt-app-launch/?utm_source=openai))
- Since then, the app has become a central access point: by mid‑2025 it had **hundreds of millions of monthly active mobile users** and, in 2025 alone, an estimated **300M+–400M+ additional downloads**, with total installs approaching 700M. ([statista.com](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1497377/global-chatgpt-vs-gemini-app-downloads/?utm_source=openai))  This mobile reach plausibly underpins much of the jump in both user count and query volume.

Putting this together:
- **User count** has increased by around **7–8×** versus the pre‑app 100M‑user baseline—not literally 10×, but close to the “roughly an order of magnitude” framing.
- **Usage volume** has jumped far **beyond 10×**, from millions of daily queries in early 2023 to billions per day by mid‑2025.

Given that his claim was qualitative (“game over… going to 10x the number of users and 10x the amount of usage”), and that both users and especially usage did, in fact, grow on roughly that scale after the official app rollout and broad availability, the fairest assessment is that the prediction was **basically right in substance**, even if the current user count falls somewhat short of an exact 10×.

predictions.explanation:
Empirical data clearly support the *premise* that the 2022–2023 mortgage‑rate spike reduced US housing mobility, but they do **not** clearly show a resulting, time‑trend increase in *resident discontent with their state or city* versus prior years.

**1. Premise: rate‑lock sharply reduced mobility**

Multiple studies show that rising mortgage rates in 2022–2023 created a strong “mortgage rate lock‑in” effect:

- FHFA finds that for each percentage point current market rates exceed a homeowner’s original rate, the probability of sale falls by 18.1%, and estimates a 57% reduction in fixed‑rate home sales in 2023 Q4 and 1.33 million “missing” sales between 2022 Q2 and 2023 Q4 due to lock‑in.
  ([fhfa.gov](https://www.fhfa.gov/research/papers/wp2403?utm_source=openai))
- NBER work by Liebersohn & Rothstein estimates rising rates in 2022–2023 reduced mobility for mortgaged households by about 16%, discouraging ~800,000 moves in one year.
  ([nber.org](https://www.nber.org/papers/w32781?utm_source=openai))
- Federal Reserve researchers similarly attribute roughly 44% of the 2021–2022 drop in moves among mortgage holders to rate lock‑in, with especially large effects on within‑metro moves (fewer local and “move‑up” moves), and smaller but non‑zero effects on moves across labor‑market areas.
  ([ideas.repec.org](https://ideas.repec.org/p/fip/fedgfe/2024-88.html?utm_source=openai))

So the “people are less able or willing to move because they’re locked into low mortgage rates” part of the prediction is strongly validated.

**2. Evidence of people feeling ‘stuck’ where they live**

There is also solid evidence of *housing‑specific* frustration:

- Realtor.com and related surveys report that about 82% of homeowners who would like to sell feel “stuck” because their current mortgage rate is lower than market rates, and more than half say they’re waiting for rates to fall before listing their homes.
  ([parealtors.org](https://www.parealtors.org/blog/many-would-be-sellers-feel-hesitant-due-to-mortgage-rates/?utm_source=openai))
- A 2024 West Shore Home survey of recent buyers (2020–2023) finds 58% of homeowners feel “stuck” or “locked in”; about 23% explicitly say they’d like to move but feel they can’t because of current rates, and over one‑third report turning down job opportunities because they can’t afford housing in a new location.
  ([westshorehome.com](https://westshorehome.com/blog/homeowners-stuck/?utm_source=openai))
- An Edelman Financial survey (reported by Realty Today) finds 36% of US homeowners, and nearly half of those under 50, say they feel *trapped* in their homes by high rates and affordability; 25% of Americans say they are not able to live where they want due to financial constraints.
  ([realtytoday.com](https://www.realtytoday.com/articles/113499/20241120/half-homeowners-under-50-feel-trapped-homes-due-mortgage-rates.htm?utm_source=openai))
- A 2024 Anytime Estimate study of movers finds that about one‑third say financial desperation forced them to move somewhere they *didn’t want*, and 20% say they’re embarrassed about where they ended up—an indicator of dissatisfaction with their current location driven by affordability.
  ([anytimeestimate.com](https://anytimeestimate.com/research/moving-trends-2025/?utm_source=openai))

These surveys show a measurable sense of being **stuck in one’s current home or neighborhood** and, for a meaningful minority, **not living where they want** because of financial and rate constraints. That’s consistent with the mechanism the predictor described.

**3. Missing piece: trend in *state/city* discontent vs prior years**

The prediction, however, is more specific: it claims that *because* people can no longer easily move, we will see a **measurable rise in resident discontent with their current states or cities, compared with earlier, higher‑mobility periods.** To validate that, we’d need:

1. A consistent, national time series on satisfaction with one’s **state or city as a place to live** (e.g., Gallup‑style “satisfied with the city or area where you live?”), covering pre‑spike years and the post‑2022 period, and
2. Evidence that discontent rose in tandem with the mortgage‑lock period, beyond what can be explained by other factors (politics, crime, broader cost‑of‑living issues, etc.).

Available data fall short on both counts:

- Urban satisfaction snapshots like Gensler’s large 2024 multi‑city survey (about 13,500 residents across 27 US cities) show **wide variation but generally high satisfaction**: for example, 78% of San Antonio residents and ~70% of Atlanta residents report being satisfied or very satisfied with their city; even lower‑scoring cities like Portland, Baltimore, and Philadelphia still have around 50–60% satisfaction. Those results show current dis/satisfaction levels but lack directly comparable pre‑2022 baselines using the same methodology, so we cannot reliably infer a *trend* attributable to mortgage lock‑in.
  ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2025/11/18/city-satisfaction-rates?utm_source=openai))
- Long‑standing polls about wanting to move to another state (e.g., Gallup’s 2013–2014 surveys, where 40–50% of residents in some states already said they’d like to leave if they could) show that substantial state‑level discontent and desire to move **predate** the recent rate spike, making it hard to say that such discontent has *increased* rather than simply persisted.
  ([thecaucusblog.com](https://www.thecaucusblog.com/2014/04/gallup-poll-half-in-illinois-want-to.html?utm_source=openai))
- Academic work using older Gallup data (e.g., 2009–2016) documents county‑level averages of satisfaction with “the city or area where you live,” but again does not extend into the 2022–2025 period in a way that would allow a clear before/after comparison tied to the rate‑lock episode.
  ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12588161/?utm_source=openai))

In short, while we can document **present‑day frustration about being unable to move** and **location mismatch** for many households, we lack a clean, consistent metric showing that *overall* discontent with one’s state or city has **risen relative to earlier high‑mobility years** because of mortgage lock‑in.

**4. Causation is also hard to isolate**

Even if we did see a rise in state/city dissatisfaction over this period, it would be difficult to attribute it primarily to reduced housing mobility rather than to other contemporaneous forces: sharp rent and home‑price increases, inflation, local crime perceptions, political polarization, and pandemic after‑effects, all of which affect how people feel about where they live irrespective of whether they can easily move.

**Conclusion**

- The *mechanism* posited—rate‑driven immobility creating frustration and a sense of being stuck—is strongly supported by data on mortgage lock‑in and homeowner sentiment.
- However, the claimed *macro‑level outcome*—a demonstrable, time‑series increase in **state or city discontent** versus pre‑spike years—cannot be established with current public evidence.

Because of that measurement and attribution gap, the prediction’s truth value is **ambiguous** rather than clearly right or wrong.

predictions.explanation:
Within 1–2 years after May 2023, U.S. commercial real estate clearly experienced **significant financial distress**, especially in offices, matching David’s prediction.

Key indicators:
- MSCI reports that the stock of *distressed* U.S. commercial properties rose for four straight quarters in 2023, reaching about **$71.8B by mid‑2023** and **$85.8B by year‑end**, with offices the largest share and over 80% of new distress in Q2 2023. ([msci.com](https://www.msci.com/research-and-insights/quick-take/distress-in-us-commercial-property-increased-further?utm_source=openai))
- Trepp and other data providers show CMBS delinquencies climbing notably over that period: overall CMBS delinquency hit **4.4% in July 2023**, with office delinquencies up more than 350 basis points since end‑2022, and by January 2024 commercial mortgage delinquency was **4.66% vs. 2.94% a year earlier**, with office loans at **6.3%** and record‑high office vacancy around **20%**. ([trepp.com](https://www.trepp.com/trepptalk/cmbs-delinquency-rate-july-2023-office-lodging-delinquencies-increase-again?utm_source=openai))
- Concrete **loan defaults and write‑downs** became widespread: Brookfield defaulted on roughly **$1.1B of debt** tied to three major downtown Los Angeles office towers in 2023, and a defaulted tower (777 Figueroa) was subsequently sold at roughly **half the outstanding debt**, a textbook fire‑sale outcome. ([therealdeal.com](https://therealdeal.com/la/2024/01/02/brookfield-dtla-towers-lead-socals-top-defaults-in-2023/?utm_source=openai))
- Distress showed up in lenders’ books: Aareal Bank reported that about **25% of its €4B U.S. office loan book went into default in 2023**, creating about **€1B of non‑performing assets**, explicitly tied to U.S. office weakness. ([ft.com](https://www.ft.com/content/de4f0675-c81f-4312-b291-f8018a2bc06d?utm_source=openai))
- More broadly, commercial property foreclosures in the U.S. jumped **117% year‑over‑year** by March 2024, reaching the highest monthly foreclosure count since 2015, again concentrated in large states like California and New York—clear evidence of mounting distress. ([credaily.com](https://www.credaily.com/briefs/cre-foreclosures-rise-drastically-as-distress-looms/?utm_source=openai))

While the share of total transactions that are formally labeled “distressed” remained a minority of overall deal volume, the combination of rapidly rising delinquencies, large‑scale loan defaults, growing pools of distressed assets, and high‑profile fire‑sale disposals within 2023–2024 is exactly the sort of **“a lot of distress” in commercial real estate** David described for the near term. On that basis, his prediction is best judged as **right**.

predictions.explanation:
Evidence to date is mixed: the *direction* of David’s call looks broadly correct (serious office‑CRE stress spilling into some banks), but the **specific scenario** he described—large numbers of vacant office towers ending up as bank‑owned REO and being liquidated at scale, causing a broad banking problem—has not clearly materialized yet, and the main refinancing “maturity wall” is still ahead.

**1. “Huge commercial real estate problem” in offices**  
San Francisco’s office market did indeed deteriorate sharply after May 2023. Reports show record or near‑record vacancy rates in 2024–25 (mid‑30% range and among the highest in the U.S.), with rents back to mid‑2010s levels and large amounts of empty space. Similar high office vacancies are noted in other major markets. 
These conditions are widely described as severe stress in the office segment of CRE, even as some AI‑driven leasing has helped at the margin. ([cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/07/08/san-franciscos-real-estate-slide-continues-as-office-vacancies-peak.html?utm_source=openai))  
So the **“huge commercial real estate problem” (in offices)** part of the quote is substantively right.

**2. Have “all these office towers” ended up owned and liquidated by banks?**  
There *are* notable cases where lenders (including insurance companies and other institutional lenders) have taken back troubled towers or been handed the keys via deed‑in‑lieu, often at very large valuation hits—for example:
- Blackstone handing back 1740 Broadway in Manhattan, where value fell from about $605M purchase price to an appraisal around $175M, wiping out lower CMBS tranches. ([chiltonreit.com](https://chiltonreit.com/2025/06/01/public-reits-are-positioned-for-trophy-office-upside-june-2025/?utm_source=openai))  
- BentallGreenOak surrendering 757 Third Avenue in Midtown East to New York Life Real Estate Investors via a deed‑in‑lieu, with the building valued at less than half its 2015 price. ([therealdeal.com](https://therealdeal.com/new-york/2025/10/31/bgo-surrenders-midtown-east-office-tower-to-avoid-foreclosure/?utm_source=openai))  
- Owners in Chicago and other cities handing suburban and secondary towers back to lenders when sales at acceptable prices proved impossible. ([therealdeal.com](https://therealdeal.com/chicago/2024/03/20/golub-alcion-surrender-office-complex-in-suburban-chicago/?utm_source=openai))  

However, system‑level data and supervisory commentary suggest **widespread bank foreclosures and fire‑sale liquidations have *not* yet happened**. A New York Fed analysis explicitly describes banks engaging in “extend‑and‑pretend”—extending CRE loan maturities to avoid crystallizing losses—leaving many problem loans in limbo instead of taking properties onto bank balance sheets and selling them. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/markets/us/ny-fed-says-banks-obscuring-commercial-real-estate-risks-by-extending-loan-terms-2024-10-23/?utm_source=openai))  
In other words, we see a growing *trickle* of lender‑takebacks and distressed sales at steep discounts, but not the wave of mass bank ownership and forced liquidation that David’s wording implies.

**3. Have CRE write‑offs become a “big banking problem”?**  
Office and broader CRE stress *has* created meaningful problems for some banks:
- New York Community Bancorp (NYCB) suffered multiple quarters of large losses, sharp rating downgrades into junk territory, and a delayed path back to profitability, largely tied to CRE and multifamily exposure—including offices. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/fitch-downgrades-new-york-community-bancorp-bb-2024-05-07/?utm_source=openai))  
- Major banks like Bank of America report significantly higher net charge‑offs driven by office loans and have elevated criticized office exposure, though office is still a small share of their total loan books. ([content.equisolve.net](https://content.equisolve.net/sec/0000070858-25-000139/bac-20241231.htm?utm_source=openai))  
- Office delinquencies in the CMBS market hit record levels (around 11–12% by late 2025), underscoring real credit stress in the office sector. ([credaily.com](https://www.credaily.com/briefs/cmbs-delinquency-hits-7-46-as-office-sector-sets-new-record/?utm_source=openai))  

At the same time, **the U.S. banking system overall does *not* look like it’s in a full‑blown crisis driven by office CRE**:
- FDIC data for Q3 2025 show U.S. banks’ aggregate profits up 13.5% year‑on‑year, with strong capital and liquidity and only 57 “problem banks,” even as CRE, especially offices, is flagged as a continuing weak spot. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/sustainability/boards-policy-regulation/us-banks-report-135-jump-profits-fdic-2025-11-24/?utm_source=openai))  
- The Federal Reserve’s April 2024 Financial Stability Report and the Office of Financial Research’s 2024 Annual Report both highlight CRE—particularly office exposure at smaller/regional banks—as a *key vulnerability*, but explicitly describe the banking sector as sound and broadly well‑capitalized, with solvency risk characterized as low overall. ([federalreserve.gov](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2024-april-financial-stability-report-overview.htm?utm_source=openai))  
- All 22 large U.S. banks comfortably passed the Fed’s 2025 stress test, which included a 30% CRE price drop scenario, indicating resilience even under severe assumed CRE losses. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/bd4c6049c0f060a6e43ec3aa229c22af?utm_source=openai))  

That pattern is more consistent with **“significant localized and prospective risk, plus a few high‑profile casualties,”** rather than with the realized, system‑wide “big banking problem” implied by the quote.

**4. Why this is judged *inconclusive* rather than right or wrong**  
Key elements of the prediction are already partly borne out:
- Severe, persistent stress in office CRE (especially in San Francisco and other major markets). ([cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/07/08/san-franciscos-real-estate-slide-continues-as-office-vacancies-peak.html?utm_source=openai))  
- Rising delinquencies and charge‑offs on office loans, and real pain at some regional banks with concentrated CRE exposure. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/us-regional-banks-weather-cre-storm-office-loans-continue-lag-2025-11-06/?utm_source=openai))  

But two core mechanisms and outcomes he specified remain unsettled as of November 2025:
- **Scale of bank takeovers & liquidations of office towers:** While there are numerous high‑profile examples of keys being handed back to lenders, much of the banking sector is still in an “extend‑and‑pretend” phase, deferring foreclosures and restructurings rather than recognizing full losses and selling collateral. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/markets/us/ny-fed-says-banks-obscuring-commercial-real-estate-risks-by-extending-loan-terms-2024-10-23/?utm_source=openai))  
- **Whether this becomes a truly “big banking problem”:** Supervisors and the IMF see CRE (especially office) as one of the main *potential* triggers for future bank stress, particularly for smaller banks, but so far the system as a whole remains profitable and well‑capitalized; CRE has not (yet) produced a broad banking crisis. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/sustainability/boards-policy-regulation/us-banks-report-135-jump-profits-fdic-2025-11-24/?utm_source=openai))  

Given that:
- The phrase “in the coming years” plausibly extends beyond 2025, into the period when large volumes of CRE loans will hit maturity and be forced to refinance or default; and
- Current data show substantial stress but not the full chain of events (mass bank ownership of towers, forced liquidations, and system‑wide banking distress),

the fairest assessment as of **late 2025** is that the prediction’s ultimate accuracy is **not yet determined**. It’s directionally on track regarding office‑CRE trouble and emerging bank‑level issues, but the more catastrophic banking‑sector outcome he foresaw has neither clearly occurred nor been definitively averted.

predictions.grok_explanation: The prediction has not materialized to the extent described. While office vacancies remain high (e.g., national rate ~20.4% in Q1 2025 per J.P. Morgan) and CRE delinquencies elevated (office CMBS at 11.08-11.8% per Trepp/Hughes Marino, bank CRE PDNA ~4% per FDIC Q3 2025), banks have largely avoided mass foreclosures on office towers in SF and major cities. Isolated cases exist (e.g., Starwood forfeited Oakland offices to Deutsche Bank in 2024; ING sold SF office loan at loss in 2025 per Wolf Street), but not 'many' bank-owned towers. Banks prefer loan extensions, modifications (up 66% YoY per St. Louis Fed), or selling notes to PE firms, per Hughes Marino (Sep 2025: 'Why Haven’t More Office Buildings Gone Into Foreclosure?'). Charge-offs remain low (0.18% CRE loans Q3 2025 per FRED/Fed), far from 'significant write-offs.' Regional banks are 'weathering the storm' with resilient portfolios and declining NPLs in some cases (Reuters Nov 2025). No 'notable problem' for banking sector; problem banks at normal 1.3% (FDIC Q3 2025). CRE impacts owners/investors more than banks systemically.
